book.title: The Great Gatsby
book.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
book.synopsis: On the lawns of Jazz-Age Long Island, the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby throws lavish parties in pursuit of a lost love — and the narrator, Nick Carraway, watches the era's glamour curdle into tragedy.

mentions.title: The Valley of Ashes
mentions.positionHint: Opening of the chapter, on the road to the city
mentions.excerpt: a fantastic farm where ashes grow like wheat into ridges and hills and grotesque gardens
mentions.whyMentioned: The grey industrial dumping ground between West Egg and Manhattan, presided over by the fading eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg — Fitzgerald's emblem of the moral wasteland beneath the era's wealth.
mentions.characterContext: Nick passes through it by train and car, unsettled by the desolation wedged between two worlds of money.

mentions.title: The Plaza Hotel
mentions.whyMentioned: The rented suite where Gatsby and Tom finally force their rivalry over Daisy into the open — the novel's emotional climax staged in impersonal, sweltering grandeur.
mentions.characterContext: Nick watches Gatsby's dream come apart in real time, unable to intervene.

mentions.title: Louisville, Kentucky
mentions.positionHint: Gatsby recounts the past to Nick
mentions.whyMentioned: Daisy's genteel Southern hometown, where a young officer named Gatsby first fell in love with her before the war — the idealized past he spends the whole novel trying to buy back.
mentions.characterContext: For Gatsby the city is less a place than a memory he believes he can repeat.

mentions.title: The Love Nest
mentions.attribution: Song · Louis A. Hirsch & Otto Harbach (1920)
mentions.positionHint: Klipspringer at the piano during the reunion
mentions.whyMentioned: The first tune Klipspringer picks out on Gatsby's piano while Gatsby and Daisy reunite — a popular song of cozy domestic bliss whose sentiment sits ironically against their impossible situation.
mentions.characterContext: Gatsby is too nervous to notice the music; the ordinary love song mocks the extraordinary one he wants.

mentions.title: Ain't We Got Fun
mentions.positionHint: Klipspringer plays on, at Gatsby's request
mentions.excerpt: One thing's sure and nothing's surer / The rich get richer and the poor get — children.
mentions.whyMentioned: The second song Klipspringer plays during the reunion — its jaunty refrain about the rich getting richer needling the class gulf that quietly dooms Gatsby and Daisy.
mentions.characterContext: The cheerful tune underlines a truth the lovers are trying not to hear.

mentions.title: Three O'Clock in the Morning
mentions.positionHint: The orchestra plays at the party Daisy attends
mentions.excerpt: a neat, sad little waltz of that year
mentions.whyMentioned: The waltz the orchestra plays at the party Daisy attends — Nick hears in it the sound of a moment already slipping into the past.
mentions.characterContext: Nick registers a melancholy the partygoers around him miss.

mentions.title: Vladimir Tostoff's Jazz History of the World
mentions.attribution: Song · performed at Gatsby's party (Fitzgerald's invention)
mentions.whyMentioned: The grandly titled orchestral premiere at Gatsby's party — a composition Fitzgerald invents to satirize the era's appetite for spectacle and self-important novelty.
mentions.characterContext: Nick, new to this world, can't tell whether the crowd is impressed or only pretending to be.

mentions.title: Simon Called Peter
mentions.positionHint: On the table in Myrtle's apartment
mentions.excerpt: a copy of 'Simon Called Peter' lay upon the table
mentions.whyMentioned: A racy 1921 bestseller lying out in Myrtle's apartment — drunk, Nick can't make sense of it, and the book's presence quietly marks the tawdry pretension of Tom and Myrtle's affair.
mentions.characterContext: Nick's growing discomfort at the party crystallizes around this small, seedy detail.

mentions.title: Hopalong Cassidy
mentions.positionHint: Produced by Gatsby's father after the funeral
mentions.whyMentioned: The old Western novel in whose flyleaf a boyhood James Gatz penciled a self-improvement schedule — produced by his grieving father as proof of the son's lifelong striving toward greatness.
mentions.characterContext: Henry Gatz offers the worn book as evidence that his son was always destined to rise.

mentions.title: The Rise of the Colored Empires
mentions.whyMentioned: The pseudo-scientific race-panic book Tom Buchanan parrots at dinner — Fitzgerald's thinly veiled nod to Lothrop Stoddard's real 1920 tract, used to expose Tom's bigotry and brittle insecurity.
mentions.characterContext: Tom repeats its ideas as settled fact, needing to believe civilization is his to defend.

mentions.title: Trimalchio (Petronius's Satyricon)
mentions.positionHint: Nick reflects as the parties end
mentions.whyMentioned: Nick likens Gatsby to Trimalchio, the vulgar newly-rich host of a lavish feast in Petronius's Roman satire — a classical mirror for Gatsby's ostentation. Fitzgerald nearly titled the novel 'Trimalchio'.
mentions.characterContext: Nick's allusion carries both admiration and a faint, knowing pity.

mentions.title: The 1919 World Series fix
mentions.positionHint: Gatsby introduces Nick to Meyer Wolfsheim
mentions.excerpt: the man who fixed the World's Series back in 1919
mentions.whyMentioned: Meyer Wolfsheim is introduced as the gambler who rigged the 1919 World Series — anchoring Gatsby's fortune to real organized crime and the decade's corrosion of even the national pastime.
mentions.characterContext: Nick is stunned that one man could 'play with the faith of fifty million people'.
